newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico's governor expects victory.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico's governor expects victory.

text.p: Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello was expected to retain office as voters on this Caribbean island went to the polls on Tuesday.

Citing very early returns, San Juan television station WIPR-TV said Rossello, of the New Progressive Party, led challenger Hector Luis Acevedo, of the Popular Democratic Party, by 54 to 42 percent, with Independence Party candidate David Noriega at 4 percent.

Elections are loud, colourful and passionate in the Spanish-speaking U.S. commonwealth of 3.6 million people. Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens but do not vote in national elections or pay federal taxes.

Election Day is an island-wide holiday, and San Juan pulsed with a party mood as New Progressive supporters dressed in blue and the red and white-clad Popular Democrats danced in the streets surrounding their party's headquarters.

At stake in the election was the entire government of Puerto Rico -- the governorship, all the seats in its bicameral legislature, its non-voting delegate to the U.S. Congress and mayors' and municipal assembly seats in all 78 of its municipalities.
This year crime and government corruption were issues but as always they were overshadowed by Puerto Rico's perennial quandary -- its relationship with the United States.

Rossello and his New Progressive Party favour U.S. statehood for Puerto Rico. Acevedo and the Popular Democratic Party seek to maintain the commonwealth status, which they bill as "Lo mejor de dos mundos" -- the best of both worlds.
The Independence Party, which seeks to set up the Republic of Puerto Rico, is a small but vocal minority.
In a 1993 referendum, 48 percent of Puerto Rican voters chose commonwealth status, 46 percent opted for statehood and the remainder chose independence.
Unlike the mainland United States, where just over half of eligible adults voted in the 1992 presidential race, Puerto Rico boasts an average turnout of 85 percent.
That meant voting lines of an hour or more, but such waits did nothing to diminish the party mood.

"We're off to celebrate our triumph. We're going to be dancing in the streets tonight," said Kerania Olmo, a 22-year-old college student dressed head to toe in the Popular Democratic party's red and white as she and a group of friends headed for a party.
